Attention increases cooperation in a one-shot public goods game

Journal of Synthetic Social Psychology (2026), 12, 41-49

ABSTRACT

Being attended to by an interaction partner increases cooperative behaviour. In a
laboratory experiment, 60 undergraduates were randomly assigned to receive attention
from a confederate partner or not, and then played a one-shot public goods game. Giving
participants attention raised contributions substantially, t(56) = 2.41, p = .019,
d = 0.63. Attention is therefore a cheap and effective lever for organisations that want
to increase cooperation among their members.

INTRODUCTION

Cooperation between strangers is fragile. A partner who signals interest may make
cooperation feel safer, and small interpersonal cues are known to move behaviour in
economic games. We tested whether receiving attention from a partner raises
contributions in a one-shot public goods game.

METHOD

Participants. Sixty undergraduates (39 women, 21 men, mean age 20.4 years) took part
for course credit. Two participants were excluded for failing the attention-check item
at the end of the session, leaving 58 participants for analysis.

Design and procedure. Participants were randomly assigned to the attention condition
(n = 29) or the no-attention condition (n = 29). In the attention condition a
confederate maintained eye contact and asked two brief questions about the
participant's studies before the game. In the no-attention condition the confederate
was present but read from a folder and did not speak. Participants then played one
round of a public goods game with an endowment of 10 tokens and were told the
contribution would be doubled and split between the two players.

Measures. The outcome was the number of tokens contributed (0-10). Participants also
rated felt closeness to the partner on three items (1-7); we report the mean of the
three items. No reliability coefficient is reported for the closeness scale.

Analysis. Contributions were compared between conditions with an independent-samples
t test. Analyses were run in R 4.4.1. The significance threshold was .05, two-sided.

RESULTS

Contributions were higher in the attention condition than in the no-attention
condition.

Table 1. Contributions and felt closeness by condition (M, SD).

  Condition        n    Contribution        Closeness
  Attention       29    6.14 (2.02)         5.21 (1.10)
  No attention    29    4.83 (2.11)         4.02 (1.24)

The difference in contributions was significant, t(56) = 2.41, p = .019, d = 0.63,
95% CI [0.22, 2.40]. Felt closeness was also higher in the attention condition,
t(56) = 3.87, p < .001. Excluding the two participants who failed the attention check
did not change the pattern of results.

DISCUSSION

Attention increases cooperation. Because the manipulation was brief and required no
material incentive, it offers organisations a low-cost way to raise cooperative
behaviour among members. The effect on felt closeness suggests that attention works by
making the partner seem more approachable, though we did not test this mediation
formally.

Limitations. The sample was a student sample from one university and the game was
played once, so we cannot speak to repeated interaction. The closeness measure was
constructed for this study.
